title: Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.1
summary: Republishes version 2.1 of PKCS #1 from RSA Laboratories, covering RSA cryptography including encryption, signatures and encoding methods. Change control stays with the PKCS process, and the text was taken from that document with some corrections. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 8017.

eli5.summary: RSA is a way to lock messages with a public key and unlock them with a private one. This note is the instruction book for doing that correctly. It was replaced by RFC 8017.

subtitle: The specification of RSA encryption and signatures: key formats, basic operations and the padding schemes that make them safe to use.

tldr.problem: Raw RSA arithmetic is not a usable security tool on its own, so implementers need agreed key formats, data conversions and padding schemes to build interoperable encryption and signatures.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #1 v2.1 defines RSA key types (including multi-prime), conversion and RSA primitives, two encryption schemes (RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5), two signature schemes with appendix (RSASSA-PSS and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) and ASN.1 syntax for keys and schemes.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational republication of an RSA Laboratories document, it obsoletes RFC 2437, and it was itself replaced by RFC 8017.

today: RFC 3447 was obsoleted by RFC 8017, so it is no longer the current version of this specification. It is Informational and itself replaced RFC 2437.

sections.title: What PKCS #1 Covers
sections.content:
This memo republishes PKCS #1 v2.1 from RSA Laboratories. Change control stays within the PKCS process, and the body is taken directly from that document with certain corrections made during RFC publication. It gives recommendations for implementing public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm, covering cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and ASN.1 syntax for representing keys and identifying schemes.

The recommendations are general and flexible, and application standards built on them may add constraints. They are intended to be compatible with IEEE Std 1363-2000. The document supersedes PKCS #1 version 2.0 but includes compatible techniques, and it is published as Informational, so it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.eli5: This is an instruction book for a famous lock-and-key system, copied from the company that wrote it.

sections.title: RSA Keys and Data Conversion
sections.content:
An RSA public key is a pair (n, e): the modulus n and the public exponent e. The modulus is a product of u distinct odd primes, with u at least 2, and e is between 3 and n - 1. This version supports multi-prime RSA, where the modulus has more than two prime factors, which lowers the cost of decryption and signing when the Chinese Remainder Theorem is used.

A private key has two allowed representations. One is the pair (n, d). The other is a quintuple (p, q, dP, dQ, qInv) plus a possibly empty sequence of triplets for any additional primes. Two conversion primitives link integers and octet strings: I2OSP turns an integer into an octet string of a given length, and OS2IP goes the other way, with the first octet the most significant.
sections.eli5: The public key is the lock anyone can use, and the private key is the secret that opens it. Two small converters turn numbers into bytes and back again.

sections.title: The Four RSA Primitives
sections.content:
The cryptographic primitives are basic mathematical operations in two pairs, and they are not intended to provide security apart from a scheme. RSAEP encrypts with c = m^e mod n and RSADP decrypts, either with m = c^d mod n or with the faster CRT form. RSASP1 signs and RSAVP1 verifies, using the same math with different roles: the signature is s = m^d mod n and verification computes m = s^e mod n.

Each primitive rejects inputs that are not between 0 and n - 1, outputting an error such as message representative out of range. The specifications also assume the keys are valid, and behavior is unspecified when they are not.
sections.eli5: There are four basic moves: lock, unlock, sign and check a signature. They are just number tricks, so on their own they are not yet safe to use.

sections.title: Encryption and Signature Schemes
sections.content:
A scheme combines primitives with an encoding step. Two encryption schemes are defined. RSAES-OAEP is recommended for new applications. It can encrypt messages of up to k - 2hLen - 2 octets, and it is described as semantically secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks under stated assumptions. RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is kept only for compatibility, is not recommended for new applications, and handles up to k - 11 octets, with its encoded message laid out as 0x00 || 0x02 || PS || 0x00 || M.

Two signature schemes with appendix are defined, meaning the message itself is needed to verify. RSASSA-PSS is recommended for eventual adoption in new applications, and it is probabilistic because it uses a random salt. RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 has no known attacks and remains appropriate for new applications, but a gradual transition to PSS is encouraged.

The text also advises using a given RSA key pair in only one scheme, since a weakness in one scheme could compromise another.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to lock a message and two ways to sign one. The newer ways are recommended because they are harder to trick, and each key should only be used for one way.

sections.title: Encoding Methods and ASN.1 Syntax
sections.content:
The signature schemes rely on encoding methods defined in Section 9: EMSA-PSS and EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5. In EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 a hash function identifier is embedded in the encoding, so an attacker cannot usefully switch to a different hash. EMSA-PSS has no such identifier, so the RFC recommends basing its mask generation function on the same hash function.

Appendix A gives ASN.1 syntax for RSA public and private keys and for identifying the schemes, and Appendix C gives a full ASN.1 module. Appendix B covers the supporting techniques. It lists six example hash functions: MD2, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. For OAEP and PSS only SHA-1 and SHA-256/384/512 are recommended, and the mask generation function used is MGF1.
sections.eli5: Before locking or signing, the message is wrapped and mixed in a set way. The book also gives the exact format for writing keys down so different programs can read them.

sections.title: Revision History and Security Notes
sections.content:
The revision history runs from versions 1.0 to 1.3, circulated in February and March 1991, through 1.4 (the June 3, 1991 initial public release) and 1.5 (republished as RFC 2313), to 2.0 (republished as RFC 2437), which introduced RSAES-OAEP and no longer allowed MD4. Version 2.1 introduces multi-prime RSA and the RSASSA-PSS signature scheme, and still supports the version 2.0 schemes.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence saying that security issues are discussed throughout the memo. The RFC also asks that any substantial use of its text acknowledge RSA Security Inc. and identify the material as 'RSA Security Inc. PKCS #1 v2.1'.
sections.eli5: The book has had several editions. This one added using more than two secret numbers and a newer way to sign, and it keeps the older ways working.
